issues.description: In the Experiment 2 results, the token-based interaction between specificity and condition is reported with z = 0.60 and p < 0.01. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55, making p < 0.01 impossible. Either the z-value or the p-value is incorrect, casting doubt on whether this token-based analysis actually supports the authors' claims.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.subcategory: discrepant values between text and table
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported differently in the text and in Table 5. The text states B = 41, t = 3.837, while Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76. Similarly for regressions-out, the text states B = 0.3, z = 3.12, while Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65. These discrepancies suggest either different models were run, an error in transcription, or unreported analytic variations. The differences are non-trivial (e.g., z = 2.65 vs. z = 3.12 implies different effect magnitudes).
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) ... The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01)

issues.description: The authors state that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should impact tasks involving 'the production of spelling,' while specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should impact 'tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning.' This is logically backwards: diagnosticity (how well spelling predicts meaning) should be relevant for reading/categorization tasks, and specificity (how well meaning predicts spelling) should be relevant for spelling production. The experiments themselves are correctly designed (diagnosticity is tested in reading tasks; specificity in the spelling task), contradicting the stated predictions.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

issues.description: The verbal description of how diagnosticity is calculated is ambiguous and, on its most natural reading, describes the wrong quantity. The text says diagnosticity is obtained by dividing 'the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' This reads as P(suffix ∩ category) / P(category), but the computed values clearly correspond to P(category | suffix) = number of words with this suffix in this category / total number of words with this suffix. The denominator should read 'total number of words ending in this suffix.'
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy in Experiment 3 is reported as 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%). These values are clearly meant to be proportions (0.86, i.e., 86%), not percentages. As written, 0.86% would mean accuracy below 1%, which would indicate participants were essentially at floor. This is a typographical/reporting error but could mislead readers.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the model includes only random intercepts for subjects: glmer(response ~ condition + (1|subject)). There is no random intercept for items (nonwords or suffixes). Given that items vary in properties beyond the fixed effect of condition, and following recommendations by Clark (1973) and Barr et al. (2013), omitting item-level random effects risks anti-conservative inference due to the failure to generalize over items.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: missing random effects for items in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the analyses are described as 'otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1,' implying only random intercepts for subjects with no random effect for items or suffixes. With 66 nonwords and 11 suffixes, omitting item-level random effects may inflate Type I error rates. This is particularly problematic given that the key manipulation is at the suffix level.
issues.quote: The analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1.

issues.description: Across all three experiments, only random intercepts are reported (for subjects and, in Experiment 3, for suffixes). No random slopes for the condition effect are included. Barr et al. (2013) recommend the maximal random effects structure justified by the design to avoid inflated Type I error rates. The within-subject congruency manipulation in all three experiments warrants at least a by-subject random slope for condition.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: unmatched number of pre-target words across conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of pre-target words differs significantly across conditions (congruent: 4.75 vs. incongruent: 5.23, p < 0.05). This is a confound for go-past times and regressions-out (the two significant measures), because more preceding words could affect the amount of syntactic context accumulated and the distance available for regressions. The authors note this difference but do not control for it in analyses or discuss its potential impact.
issues.quote: the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05)

issues.description: In Experiment 3, six eye-movement measures are tested for the congruency effect without any correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR). While the authors argue these measures reflect different processing stages, they are computed from the same data and are likely correlated (e.g., go-past time includes first-pass dwell time), increasing the family-wise Type I error rate.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: Despite having specific hypotheses about which constructs (diagnosticity, specificity) should affect which tasks, no pre-registration is reported. The exploratory nature of the eye-tracking measures in Experiment 3 is explicitly acknowledged ('We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected'). The absence of pre-registration, combined with the sign-transformation of diagnosticity in Experiment 1, the choice of which measures to highlight, and the post-hoc exploration of diagnosticity as a moderator, raises concerns about undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation

issues.description: No power analyses are reported for any of the three experiments. Sample sizes (46, 29, and 47 participants) appear to have been determined by convenience rather than by formal consideration of expected effect sizes. Experiment 2 in particular has only 29 participants. For the suffix-level moderation analyses, statistical power may be severely limited given the small number of suffixes (10-20) contributing data.
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.

issues.subcategory: non-significant simple effects with significant interaction
issues.description: In the go-past time diagnosticity moderation analysis (Experiment 3), the interaction between diagnosticity and congruency is significant, but neither simple effect reaches significance: congruent condition p > 0.5, incongruent condition p = 0.13. The authors interpret this as support for their hypothesis, but the pattern is ambiguous when neither constituent simple effect is reliable. The claim that diagnosticity modulates go-past times in the incongruent condition rests on a marginal trend.
issues.quote: there was no effect of diagnosticity on go-past times in the congruent condition (B = 8.30, t = 0.634, p > 0.5), whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13)

issues.subcategory: high rate of missing data in Experiment 1
issues.description: 11.7% of data points in Experiment 1 were missing due to timeouts or invalid button presses. This is a high rate for a simple two-alternative forced-choice task with a 2-second window. The authors do not report whether missingness was related to condition (noun vs. adjective suffixes), suffix diagnosticity, or individual participant characteristics. Non-random missingness could bias the observed effects.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.subcategory: inclusion of pseudoaffixed words in corpus measures
issues.description: The computation of diagnosticity and specificity includes pseudoaffixed words (e.g., CORNER for –ER, VANISH for –ISH). While the authors justify this by citing evidence that readers parse such words morphologically, including pseudoaffixed words could distort the statistics. Words like CORNER are nouns but ER is coded as a noun-diagnostic suffix; however, the pseudo-suffix in CORNER is not functioning as a morpheme. This inflates the apparent regularity in the corpus while potentially misrepresenting what regularities are actually available to readers.
issues.quote: we also needed to capture words in which the suffix spellings do not function as genuine morphemes (e.g. the –ER in 'corner'). ... We included pseudoaffixed words because there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these

issues.subcategory: implicit statistical learning claims without evidence
issues.description: The authors claim that the observed sensitivity to spelling-meaning regularities was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' and that 'the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction.' However, the cross-sectional design cannot distinguish between explicit and implicit learning, nor can it establish when or how this knowledge was acquired. Participants may have received explicit instruction about suffix categories, or the knowledge may arise through other mechanisms.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.description: All participants across three experiments were undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London. This limits generalizability to other populations (different ages, educational backgrounds, L2 speakers, etc.). The authors do not acknowledge this limitation. Given claims about 'skilled readers' in general, the restriction to a young, highly-educated university sample is relevant.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.description: The authors note that 'Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity.' In fact, diagnosticity as computed (P(category | suffix)) is identical to cue validity, and specificity as computed (P(suffix | category & sound sequence)) is analogous to category validity or cue-category association strength. The claim that these are 'new constructs' overstates their novelty. While their application to the spelling-meaning domain is new, the mathematical formulations are established in the categorization literature.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964).

issues.description: In the computational analysis, 64 suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words were excluded for a robustness check, leaving 95 suffixes (stated) from an initial 154. However, 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. This arithmetic discrepancy suggests either the exclusion criterion or the reported numbers are incorrect.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes ... For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.subcategory: no participant exclusion criteria for comprehension
issues.description: In Experiment 3, comprehension accuracy ranged from 66% to 98%. No participants appear to have been excluded based on low comprehension accuracy, despite 66% being close to chance for yes/no questions (50%). Low comprehension suggests some participants may not have been reading the sentences attentively, which would add noise and could differentially affect conditions.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the diagnosticity variable was multiplied by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes before entering it into the model. This transformation is unusual and its justification is unclear. Different coding schemes (e.g., centering, contrast coding) could yield different results. The authors acknowledge concern about this by running separate analyses, but the primary analysis relies on this transformation.
issues.quote: we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: Token-based analyses are mentioned briefly for all three experiments but reported with minimal detail. In Experiment 1, the token effect on adjective suffixes is merely noted as 'p > 0.8' without full statistics. In Experiment 2, the token analysis contains the z = 0.60, p < 0.01 error. The systematic pattern of weaker token effects is discussed post-hoc but the full token analyses are not reported, making it impossible to evaluate these claims.
issues.quote: The results based on token measures were similar (main effect of diagnosticity, and an effect of diagnosticity on noun-diagnostic suffixes), but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity (p > 0.8).

issues.subcategory: lexical category as proxy for meaning
issues.description: The paper characterizes the relationship between spelling and 'meaning' but operationalizes meaning exclusively as lexical category (noun, adjective, verb). Lexical category is a syntactic rather than semantic property. While the authors briefly acknowledge this by citing Baayen et al. (2011), the title and framing ('meaningful regularities') suggest a broader characterization of meaning than is actually studied. The claims about 'spelling-meaning mapping' are thus narrower than presented.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of "meaning").

issues.subcategory: potential confound from verb fillers in Experiment 3
issues.description: Experiment 3 includes 40 verb-filler nonwords in addition to 80 experimental noun/adjective nonwords, but these fillers are explicitly not analyzed 'because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' The inclusion of these fillers means participants encounter verb contexts, but only noun and adjective contexts are analyzed. This could create an asymmetry in the analyzed data if participants' strategies are influenced by the full set of items they encounter.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category

issues.subcategory: missing details on list assignment in Experiment 3
issues.description: Experiment 3 uses two lists (each nonword appears in congruent context in one list and incongruent in the other), but the text does not specify how participants were assigned to lists, whether assignment was randomized, or how many participants saw each list. List is not mentioned as a factor in the analyses.
issues.quote: List 2 was identical, but nonwords that were presented in congruent contexts in List 1 were presented in their corresponding incongruent contexts, and vice versa.

issues.subcategory: overclaiming about English writing system evolution
issues.description: The authors argue that 'the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional' and that spelling-sound inconsistency 'maximises the transmission of meaningful information.' While the entropy analysis shows a statistically significant difference (slope of 0.9 vs. 1), the actual difference in mean entropy between spelling (0.61) and phonology (0.63) is very small. The strong evolutionary claims about English spelling becoming fractionated to maximize meaning transmission go substantially beyond what a 0.02 difference in entropy supports.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).
